Koh Samui has Muay Thai camps for complete beginners and for serious fighters, with drop-in group classes from about 500 THB, weekly packages of about 2,500–3,000 THB and monthly memberships of about 7,500–10,000 THB in 2026. To watch, two stadiums in Chaweng share six fight nights a week (none on Thursday), with tickets at 1,500, 2,000 and 2,500 THB. This page covers training; stadium details are on our Muay Thai fight nights page.

Training for beginners

You don't need to be fit or experienced to start. Group classes on Samui are mixed-level, and trainers split beginners off for technique work while experienced students spar. A typical first class runs like this:

  1. 15 min Skipping rope and stretching to warm up.
  2. 15 min Shadow boxing: stance, guard, the basic jab, cross, teep (push kick) and roundhouse kick.
  3. 30–45 min Pad work with a trainer, usually 3–5 rounds of 3 minutes, one to one.
  4. 15 min Bag work and clinch drills.
  5. 15 min Conditioning (sit-ups, push-ups) and cool-down.

Go at your own pace. Trainers adjust the intensity, and you can sit out a round. Most beginners find two or three sessions a week plenty for the first week, because the heat is the hardest part: daytime highs on Samui are 29–33 °C all year, and gyms are open-air.

What to bring

  • Shorts and a quick-dry T-shirt (many camps sell Muay Thai shorts for a few hundred baht).
  • Hand wraps; buy your own for hygiene, they cost little.
  • Gloves and shin guards are usually available to borrow; regular students buy their own.
  • Two litres of water and electrolyte sachets from any 7-Eleven.
  • A small towel. You train barefoot.

Choosing a camp: visit before you pay for a month. Watch a class, check the ratio of trainers to students (one trainer to four or five students is good), the condition of the mats and bags, and whether beginners get proper pad time or just stand at the bag. Camps in Chaweng and Bophut are the most convenient if you are staying in the north-east; Lamai has quieter, more traditional gyms. We can recommend a camp to suit your level: message us.

A typical training week

Most Samui camps follow a similar weekly rhythm. Sunday is usually the rest day, and some camps close on Sunday entirely. A sensible first week for a beginner looks like this:

DayMorning sessionAfternoon sessionBeginner tip
MondayTechnique and padsRestLearn stance and guard; don't overdo it
TuesdayRestTechnique and padsAfternoon heat is easier after 16:00
WednesdayTechnique, bag and clinchRestYour shins will be sore; that is normal
ThursdayRest or light runTechnique and padsThe only night with no stadium fights
FridayTechnique and conditioningRestWatch a fight in Chaweng that evening
SaturdayLight pads or a private lessonRestMany camps run shorter Saturday sessions
SundayRestRestMassage, beach or a boat day

By the second week most beginners can train once a day, and fit visitors move to two sessions a day. Listen to the trainers. The most common beginner mistake is training twice a day from day one, then spending the rest of the week too sore to train at all.

Muay Thai words you will hear

  • Wai kru ram muay: the ritual dance fighters perform before a bout to honour their teachers. Watch for it at the stadium.
  • Mongkhon and prajiad: the headband and armbands worn for the ritual; the mongkhon is removed before the fight starts.
  • Teep: the push kick, used to keep distance. One of the first techniques you learn.
  • Khao and sok: knee and elbow strikes, which make Muay Thai "the art of eight limbs".
  • Clinch: grappling at close range to land knees and throw the opponent off balance.
  • Sarama: the live music of pipe and drums played during fights, which speeds up as the action builds.

Private lessons

A private lesson is the fastest way to learn the basics. You get a full session of pad work and correction with one trainer, usually for an hour. Expect from about 1,000 THB per session in 2026, with discounts for packs of five or ten. Privates suit couples and families with older children, people with injuries who need a gentler approach, and anyone preparing for a first fight.

Training on a long stay: the DTV visa

Thailand's Destination Thailand Visa (DTV) has a "soft power" track that covers Muay Thai courses. The key terms in 2026:

  • Valid for 5 years, multiple entry, with stays of up to 180 days per entry.
  • One in-country extension of 180 days, for 1,900 THB.
  • Visa fee 10,000 THB; proof of 500,000 THB in savings.
  • You apply online from outside Thailand, with an acceptance letter from the Muay Thai school.
  • Since 31 August 2026 you apply via the Thai mission for your nationality or residence, and a criminal record certificate is required.
  • You may not work for a Thai employer on a DTV.

Rules change often, so check the official e-visa site and our Thailand visa guide before you commit to a long camp. Since 15 September 2026, visa-exempt visitors from most Western countries get 30 days on arrival instead of 60.

Health and safety

  • Heat: train early or late, drink before you are thirsty and stop if you feel dizzy. March to May is the hottest period (highs 30–33 °C).
  • Injuries: shins, toes, wrists and ribs take the most knocks. Wrap your hands properly and don't spar until a trainer says you are ready.
  • Skin: cover cuts and blisters, because infections spread quickly in humid, shared gyms.
  • Insurance: many travel policies exclude contact sports or competitive fighting. Read the exclusions before you train, and before any fight. See travel insurance for Koh Samui.
  • Hospitals: the main private hospitals are in Chaweng and Bophut; ambulance 1669. See hospitals on Koh Samui.
  • Roads: many students ride scooters to the gym. You need a licence with a motorcycle category, and the helmet fine is up to 2,000 THB. See motorbike rental.

How to book

We don't run a gym ourselves. We match you with a camp that suits your level, location and budget, and pass on the camp's own prices. Message us on WhatsApp with your dates, where you are staying, your experience, and your choice of group classes or privates, and we will reply with options. Tell us about any injuries too, so we can suggest a camp or trainer used to working around them. Prices are paid to the camp in THB, usually in cash on your first day.
